newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica officials sanguine about impact of fx move.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica officials sanguine about impact of fx move.

text.p: South Africa's top economic officials said on Wednesday they were confident that the easing of exchange controls on individuals from July 1 would not create any undue problems.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said the move would not disrupt interest rate policy. His deputy, James Cross, estimated that between three and five billion rand could leave the country following the latest relaxation of capital controls, but this would be roughly matched by inflows.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said the 200,000 rand limit for individual investments, announced earlier, was a one-off allowance, but he expected the cap to be increased over time.
"The chances are good that you will see little, if any, decline in foreign reserves. The level of interest rates should not be affected by this," Stals said at a news conference.
The central bank governor said local liquidity constraints would limit the amount of money which individual South Africans would take offshore.
Stals said the Reserve bank had access to 38 billion rand in official reserves and credit lines which could be used to supply liquidity to the market in the event of a significant flight of capital.
Stals said that relaxing controls for emigrants, possibly by issuing bonds to free their cash gradually, was not an immediate priority.
"It is a theoretical possibility but it is not seriously considered at this stage," he said.

Some 10-15 billion rand of so-called "blocked rands" belonging to emigrants are currently locked up in South Africa. Given that the owners of the money have moved abroad, all this money could be expected to leave the country once controls on it are freed.
Manuel added he was not in a position to announce an amnesty for those South Africans who had illegally taken their money offshore in contravention of exchange controls.
